extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP lawyers, law students and counsel assessing damages
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and quantifying a reasonable royalty in US patent litigation by applying the Georgia-Pacific factors (the multi-factor framework for hypothetical negotiation and royalty calculation). Useful for damages experts, counsel, and courts determining license rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: reasonable royalty as damages baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the bases for an award of damages in most jurisdictions is at least a “reasonable royalty,” i.e., not less than the royalty the infringer would have paid for a license of the patent at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Georgia-Pacific case listed factors courts may use to determine a reasonable royalty; these factors are widely cited in patent litigation but are criticized for treating products as if they required only one patent and for ignoring royalty stacking in complex high-technology products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 1: royalties received by the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: “The royalties received by the patentee for the licensing of the patent in suit, proving or tending to prove an established royalty.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 2: comparable patent license rates
rubrics_metrics.description: “The rates paid by the licensee for the use of other patents comparable to the patent in suit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare licenses for patents similar in technology, scope, and commercial context to infer a market royalty rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 3: nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: “The nature and scope of the license, as exclusive or non-exclusive; or as restricted or non-restricted in terms of territory or with respect to whom the manufactured product may be sold.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider exclusivity, territorial restrictions, field-of-use limitations, and other license contours that affect value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 4: licensor’s licensing policy and marketing program
rubrics_metrics.description: “The licensor’s established policy and marketing program to maintain his patent monopoly by not licensing others to use the invention or by granting licenses under special conditions designed to preserve that monopoly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate patentee practices (e.g., refusal to license, selective licensing) that preserve exclusivity and thus can raise royalty expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 5: commercial relationship between licensor and licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: “The commercial relationship between the licensor and licensee, such as, whether they are competitors in the same territory in the same line of business; or whether they are inventor and promoter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for prior business dealings, competition, or special relationships that influence bargaining leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 6: convoyed sales and promotion effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “The effect of selling the patented specialty in promoting sales of other products of the licensee; the existing value of the invention to the licensor as a generator of sales of his non-patented items; and the extent of such derivative or convoyed sales.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the patented feature drives sales of other (non-patented) products or services and whether that increases the patent's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 7: patent duration and license term
rubrics_metrics.description: “The duration of the patent and the term of the license.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter remaining patent life or license term can reduce royalty; longer terms generally increase value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 8: established profitability, commercial success, popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The established profitability of the product made under the patent; its commercial success; and its current popularity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of commercial success and profitability supports higher royalties, subject to apportionment considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 9: utility and advantages over prior modes
rubrics_metrics.description: “The utility and advantages of the patent property over the old modes or devices, if any, that had been used for working out similar results.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess incremental technical or functional advantages the invention provides compared to prior solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 10: nature and commercial embodiment of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: “The nature of the patented invention; the character of the commercial embodiment of it as owned and produced by the licensor; and the benefits to those who have used the invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the invention is embodied in products, its commercial form, and the realized benefits to users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 11: extent of infringer’s use and probative value of that use
rubrics_metrics.description: “The extent to which the infringer has made use of the invention; and any evidence probative of the value of that use.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify how extensively the accused infringer exploited the invention and any measurable value derived from that exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 12: customary portion of profit or selling price
rubrics_metrics.description: “The portion of the profit or of the selling price that may be customary in the particular business or in comparable businesses to allow for the use of the invention or analogous inventions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use industry norms and comparable business practices to inform what portion of revenue is customarily allocated to IP usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 13: apportionment to the invention versus other factors
rubrics_metrics.description: “The portion of the realizable profit that should be credited to the invention as distinguished from non-patented elements, the manufacturing process, business risks, or significant features or improvements added by the infringer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully apportion profits to the patented invention itself and exclude value from unpatented features, processes, business efforts, and infringer-added improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 14: opinion testimony of qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert economic and technical testimony is a recognized input to establish reasonable royalty components and apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 15: hypothetical negotiation / bargaining range
rubrics_metrics.description: “The amount that a licensor (such as the patentee) and a licensee (such as the infringer) would have agreed upon (at the time the infringement began) if both had been reasonably and voluntarily trying to reach an agreement; that is, the amount that a prudent licensee—who desired, as a business proposition, to obtain a license to manufacture and sell a particular article embodying the patented invention—would have been willing to pay as a royalty and yet be able to make a reasonable profit and which amount would have been acceptable by a prudent patentee who was willing to grant a license.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core hypothetical negotiation framework: frame the damages as what the parties would have agreed upon ex ante, considering commercial realities, bargaining positions, and the need for the licensee to make a reasonable profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: entire market value rule caution
rubrics_metrics.description: “Recent case law has also limited the ability of an infringer to assert that a royalty should be based on the ‘entire market value’ of the accused product or service, based on infringement by a single feature of many in the infringing product.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base a royalty on the entire market value of a multi-feature product unless the patented feature drives the demand for the entire product (i.e., meets the entire market value rule/technical nexus requirements); courts require careful proof of the patented feature's value relative to the whole product.
